introduction: “The imitator saith that such a man hath seen, such a man hath heard … he dependeth upon the sight, the hearing and the conscience of others.” Taqlíd, the following of ancestors and religious authorities without examination, is for these readings the chief reason that each Messenger was denied and the chief cause of division among religions: “imitation differs but reality … is one.” The sixty-five readings state the duty to see with one’s own eyes, describe how belief is inherited and how leaders stand between people and the light, trace the consequences (apathy, irreligion, conflict), and end with the image, used again and again by Bahá’u’lláh, of chains broken. The Qur’án’s “we found our fathers following a religion” is the text behind many of them; Jesus on the tradition of men and blind leaders of the blind, the Buddha to the Kalamas, Socrates, Descartes, Kant, Milton, Mill, Emerson and Whitman say the same in their own settings. The case for tradition deserves a hearing too, and gets one here from Chesterton, Burke, Proverbs and the opening of the Mishnah; and Paine and Emerson raise the question of whether rejecting imitation leaves a person with anything but himself.
questions: “He dependeth upon the sight, the hearing and the conscience of others.” Which of your convictions have you examined for yourself, and which do you hold because those around you hold them?
The readings warn against imitation and, in the same breath, against following “your own selves.” How is independent investigation different from Paine’s “my own mind is my own church”?
Chesterton calls tradition “the democracy of the dead,” and the Mishnah begins with a chain of transmission. What is the difference between receiving a tradition and imitating it?
“Imitation differs but reality … is one.” Milton expected free inquiry to produce “many opinions.” On what grounds do the readings expect it to unite?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá advises going “to the other churches and mosques.” What have you learned of your own belief by sitting in someone else’s place of worship?
“Now again has the cycle of blind imitation begun to move.” How does a community founded on breaking with imitation guard against imitating its own founders?

outside.why: The imitator “dependeth upon the sight, the hearing and the conscience of others.” Milton: a man may be a heretic in the truth; if he believe things only because his pastor says so, the very truth he holds becomes his heresy.
Job at the end of his trial marks the difference between the two kinds of knowing: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.
That people “observe and hearken with their own eyes and ears.” Kant, a century earlier: have courage to use your own reason!
Whitman: you shall no longer take things at second or third hand, nor look through the eyes of the dead. You shall not look through my eyes either.
“Set thou aside that which thou hast heard from fathers and ancestors.” The Buddha to the Kalamas: don’t go by reports, by legends, by traditions, by scripture.
Descartes’ first rule: never to accept anything for true which I did not clearly know to be such.

“Follow not your own selves, but follow the ways of God.” Paine’s independence ends in himself: my own mind is my own church. What distinguishes seeing with one’s own eyes from following one’s own fancies?

Emerson: imitation is suicide; a man must take himself for better, for worse, as his portion. The reading warns against “idle fancies” in the same breath as imitation. Is Emerson’s self-reliance what the readings ask for?
“Each must see with his own eyes, hear with his own ears, and investigate truth.” Paul: prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
The Qur’án makes the same faculties answerable: follow not that whereof thou hast no knowledge. Lo! the hearing and the sight and the heart, of each of these it will be asked.
To be rid of imitations “so that your thoughts and minds will be broadened.” Paul: be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind.
Go even “to the other churches and mosques.” Mark Twain: travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness.
Ibn ‘Arabí: my heart has become capable of every form: a convent for Christian monks, the pilgrim’s Ka‘ba, the tables of the Tora and the book of the Koran.
A man is a Jew because his father was. Pascal on the geography of conviction: truth on this side of the Pyrenees, error on the other.
Locke: of all the men we meet with, nine parts of ten are what they are by their education.
Each nation imagined that the law of God demanded ancestral forms. Montaigne: every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country.
“All religions have gradually become bound by tradition and dogma.” Jesus: laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men.

Chesterton defends what the readings attack: tradition means giving votes to the most obscure of all classes, our ancestors. It is the democracy of the dead. What does tradition preserve that an inquirer starting from nothing would lose?
Religious leaders “suppose that religion consists of blind imitation of one’s ancestors.” Isaiah: their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men.
People “inherit their belief from parents and ancestors and follow it blindly.” Peter to his converts: your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers.
The reading quotes the Qur’án: we found our fathers following a religion, and we are guided by their footprints.
And the Qur’án’s answer: what! Even though their fathers were wholly unintelligent and had no guidance?
“We find not this in the books of our forefathers.” Jeremiah foresees nations saying the opposite: surely our fathers have inherited lies, vanity, and things wherein there is no profit.
The answer given to every messenger. The Qur’án: We sent not a warner before thee into any township but its luxurious ones said: Lo! we found our fathers following a religion.
“They see through the eyes of their leaders.” Jesus: they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
“We deny what the leader denieth.” The Qur’án gives the same people’s words at the end: Our Lord! we obeyed our princes and great men, and they misled us from the Way.
The heads of religions “have captured the souls of man.” The Qur’án: they have taken as lords beside Allah their rabbis and their monks.
Jesus to his own disciples, lest they repeat the pattern: be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ.

The masses trust the famous, and suppose that “imitating any scholar or learned person” leads to truth. Bacon noticed that the current also runs the other way: in all superstition wise men follow fools.
Elihu, the youngest speaker in Job: great men are not always wise: neither do the aged understand judgment.
People asked Pharaoh who Moses was, and the Pharisees who Jesus was. Philip’s answer to Nathanael’s prejudice was shorter: come and see.
“Those who claimed knowledge closed their eyes.” Paul describes himself before Damascus: being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers.

People “as sheep led by their shepherd whithersoever he willeth.” Emerson: society everywhere is in conspiracy against the manhood of every one of its members. The virtue in most request is conformity.
Who are the imitators and who the people of insight? Luke’s example of the second: they searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Not People of the Book but “followers of blind imitation.” The Samaritans, on the day their belief became their own: now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves.
They “raise a lifeless cry and worship their own vain imaginings.” Jesus: making the word of God of none effect through your tradition.
Discussion with those who “speak with rules and proofs” is easy. Socrates: the life which is unexamined is not worth living.

Ministers “have taught that religion is opposed to science and reason and have thus enforced imitation.” Mill: however true it may be, if it is not fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed, it will be held as a dead dogma, not a living truth.

In France, imitation enforced by religious leaders produced irreligion. Emerson to divinity students: men have come to speak of the revelation as somewhat long ago given and done, as if God were dead.
“The initiator is of course superior to the imitator.” Thoreau: if a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer.
From ignorance based on imitation “wars and battles prevail.” Saxe’s blind men and the elephant: the disputants rail on in utter ignorance, and prate about an Elephant not one of them has seen.
Imitations “have concealed the Sun of Reality.” Xenophanes, the first to say how gods come to resemble their worshippers: horses would paint the forms of the gods like horses, and oxen like oxen.
“Differences between religions are due to misunderstanding and imitation.” Jesus removes the titles on which inherited loyalties hang: all ye are brethren; and call no man your father upon the earth.

“If the nations … would abandon imitation and investigate reality, all would become united.” Milton expected investigation to multiply opinions first: where there is much desire to learn, there of necessity will be much arguing, many opinions; for opinion in good men is but knowledge in the making. How do the readings expect inquiry to end in unity?
“The removal of religious imitations” stands in a list of the age’s needs. Tennyson: the old order changeth, yielding place to new, lest one good custom should corrupt the world.
Some people are “like unto the spiders”: tear the web and they spin again. Jeremiah on the grip of habit: can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?
People “drowning in the sea of imitation, having no insight of their own.” Plato’s prisoners: they see only their own shadows, which the fire throws on the opposite wall of the cave.
“Running after dogmas … following the creed of ancestors.” Paul: beware lest any man spoil you after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world.
“How long these superannuated ideas?” Emerson: our age is retrospective. It builds the sepulchres of the fathers. Why should not we also enjoy an original relation to the universe?
Misconceptions “weaker than spider’s web.” The Qur’án: the frailest of all houses is the spider’s house.

Asked for proof, “they say what their forefathers said before.” Ezekiel abolishes a proverb of inheritance: the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge. Ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb.

“Now again has the cycle of blind imitation begun to move.” Burke thought the old habit had its uses: we cherish our prejudices, and the longer they have lasted, the more we cherish them. Why does imitation return even among those who once broke with it?
They imprison “him who has broken the chains of blind imitation.” What astonished the crowds in Jesus: he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.

“Beware lest … blind imitation prevent thee.” Joshua reminded Israel that their own founder had been a breaker of tradition: your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood, and they served other gods.
To “break the chains of imitation with the strength of certitude.” Thoreau: I wished to live deliberately, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.

Blessed is the soul whom “the chains of blind imitation” have not held back. Paul: stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
“Cast behind thee the kingdom of blind imitation.” Proverbs: remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set. How would you tell a landmark from a chain?
One who has shattered “the chains of blind imitation and the idols.” Paul to Thessalonica: ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God.
Some “clung to vain imaginings,” others “hastened unto Him with clear certitude.” The Qur’án’s praise of the second: who hear advice and follow the best thereof.

People who “have cast behind them the books of the learned.” The Mishnah opens with a chain of faithful handing-on: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders. Is every handing-on imitation? What do the readings themselves ask to be handed on?
Freed from “thorn and thistle-like dogmas,” the seeker attains truth. John: believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.
A Light that “saveth the people from the darkness of blind imitations.” Xenophanes: by seeking they find in time what is better.
“This is not an age of blind imitation; it is the age of light.” Milton: let her and Falshood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the wors, in a free and open encounter?

“Decaying outdated blind imitations” must go. Bildad to Job: enquire, I pray thee, of the former age; for we are but of yesterday, and know nothing. What is the right use of the past for someone who refuses to imitate it?
That the religions “cast off the garment of blind imitation and put on the robe of truth.” Emerson: a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds.

quran-we-found-our-fathers.text: And even so We sent not a warner before thee (Muhammad) into any township but its luxurious ones said: Lo! we found our fathers following a religion, and we are following their footprints.

ezekiel-fathers-have-eaten-sour-grapes.text: What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge? As I live, saith the Lord God, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die

jeremiah-our-fathers-have-inherited-lies.text: O Lord, my strength, and my fortress, and my refuge in the day of affliction, the Gentiles shall come unto thee from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Surely our fathers have inherited lies, vanity, and things wherein there is no profit

peter-received-by-tradition-from-your-fa.text: Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers

galatians-zealous-of-the-traditions.text: And profited in the Jews' religion above many my equals in mine own nation, being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers

john-we-have-heard-him-ourselves.text: And said unto the woman, Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world

milton-heretic-in-the-truth.text: A man may be a heretic in the truth; and if he believe things only because his pastor says so, or the Assembly so determines, without knowing other reason, though his belief be true, yet the very truth he holds, becomes his heresy
milton-heretic-in-the-truth.author: John Milton

whitman-second-or-third-hand.text: You shall no longer take things at second or third hand, nor look through the eyes of the dead, nor feed on the spectres in books, / You shall not look through my eyes either, nor take things from me, / You shall listen to all sides and filter them from your self
whitman-second-or-third-hand.author: Walt Whitman

thoreau-different-drummer.text: If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer. Let him step to the music which he hears, however measured or far away
thoreau-different-drummer.author: Henry David Thoreau

galatians-stand-fast-in-liberty.text: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage
